gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the EG4 6000XP's 6,000 W is split across two 120 V legs with at most 3,000 W continuous on either one, and the unit does not balance load between legs. So on 120 V loads alone it is effectively a 3 kW inverter, not the 6 kW shown in ChatGPT's 'Small off-grid home 3–5 kW / Medium 5–8 kW' table.
standout_why: I compared against the cited EG4 product page, which says only 'split-phase 120/240V output'. I also checked wildjoule.com/best-off-grid-inverter (2026-10-17), which says outright that it does not give per-leg limits, plus storyofsolar.com's 2026 ranking, solarspecdb.com/inverters/eg4-6000xp (2026-09-02), liveoffthegrid.com/specs/inverters/eg4-6000xp and Signature Solar's 6000XP page. They state 6,000 W, a 12,000 W surge (wildjoule, storyofsolar and liveoffthegrid add about 3.5 s) and, on some pages, about 50 W idle. None of them gives the 3,000 W per-line cap. The surge duration is already on rival pages, so it does not count as new.
decides: This confirms the 6000XP for homes with a real 240 V load such as a well pump or minisplit, where both legs share the work. It weakens the pick for a 120 V-only cabin or RV, where everything sits on the two 120 V legs and any single leg tops out at 3,000 W. That puts the 6000XP in ChatGPT's own '3–5 kW' bracket for those buyers, so the page should tell them to plan wiring by leg, not by the 6 kW total. I could not open per-leg ratings for the Growatt SPE 6000 or the Sun Gold Power units, so I can't yet say whether a rival does better on one leg.

findings.label: Idle consumption by source (the condition behind the headline figure)
